query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg‐containing lightweight HEAs, there exists a kinetic threshold during thermal exposure that regulates the nucleation and spatial distribution of early intermetallic precipitates. When thermal exposure is moderate (time/temperature below the threshold), limited, finely dispersed intermetallic particles form that promote the nucleation of protective passivating oxides (e.g., TiOx, MgO), thereby retaining good corrosion and oxidation resistance. In contrast, extended or higher thermal exposures lower kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion, causing these intermetallics to coalesce into continuous networks that act as micro‐galvanic sites and compromise the protective behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy produced in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state (e.g., with elements such as Al, Be, Mg, Ti along with a minor species such as Cu or Si)
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled thermal treatments that vary in both temperature and duration to simulate different service conditions
generation.conditions: Isothermal holds at temperatures representative of service regimes (e.g., a moderate exposure around 350–400 °C relevant for corrosion conditions and higher exposures around 650–750 °C relevant for high-temperature oxidation) with treatment times ranging from short (≈1 hour) to extended (≈10 hours)
generation.structural_mediator: The nucleation density and spatial distribution of early-stage intermetallic precipitates (for instance, phases like Mg2Si or Ti2Zn) that evolve within the SS matrix
generation.mechanism: Under moderate thermal exposure, limited atomic mobility results in the formation of discrete, finely distributed intermetallic precipitates. These act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for forming thin, protective oxide films, thus undergirding corrosion and oxidation resistance. If the alloy is exposed to higher temperatures or prolonged times, enhanced diffusion leads to the coalescence and growth of intermetallic compounds into interconnected networks. Such continuous intermetallic structures promote microgalvanic coupling, undermining the integrity of the passive oxide layer and accelerating corrosion/oxidation degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to moderate thermal treatment will retain a microstructure marked by isolated intermetallic particles and will exhibit low corrosion current densities and slow high-temperature oxidation rates. Conversely, samples exposed to longer or hotter treatments will show coarser, interconnected intermetallic networks accompanied by increased corrosion current densities and more rapid oxide scale spallation or growth.
generation.baseline: The as-processed metastable solid-solution state, with its originally homogeneous element distribution and minor or no intermetallic precipitation, serves as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: The beneficial microstructure (discrete intermetallics and high passivation quality) is maintained only within a specific thermal exposure window. Exposures above a critical combination of temperature and time (e.g., >400 °C for corrosion-relevant exposure and >750 °C for oxidation-relevant exposure) are expected to trigger deleterious intermetallic coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thermal thresholds and diffusion kinetics governing the transition from dispersed to coalesced intermetallics remain uncertain. This hypothesis extends kinetic phase transformation insights from studies on HEAs (e.g., PMC5043342::web::016::kinetic_effect_and_tailoring_phases_in_c) and protective oxide formation observations (PMC12299034::web::030::3_5_general_discussion) to a Mg-containing system, an extrapolation that has not been directly verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical Mg-containing HEA samples in the metastable solid-solution state. Divide them into groups to be subjected to various controlled thermal treatments: one group undergoes a moderate thermal exposure (e.g., 350–400 °C for 1–2 hours) and another group undergoes an extended/high-temperature exposure (e.g., 650–750 °C for 8–10 hours). Use in situ TEM (with EDS mapping) to monitor the evolution of intermetallic precipitation and its spatial distribution over time. Subsequently, assess corrosion performance via potentiodynamic polarization tests and evaluate high-temperature oxidation behavior by measuring weight gain and analyzing oxide scale morphology (using XRD, SEM, and XPS).
measurements: TEM imaging and EDS mapping of intermetallic phases (discrete versus coalesced morphology)
XRD phase identification of intermetallic compounds
Corrosion current density and potential from potentiodynamic polarization testing
Weight gain measurements and oxide scale analysis (via SEM, XPS) after oxidation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal treatments that induce a transition from a discrete to a continuous intermetallic network do not correlate with a significant deterioration in corrosion resistance (e.g., increased corrosion current density) or high-temperature oxidation performance (e.g., faster oxide spallation or higher mass gain), then the proposed kinetic threshold mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Among these systems, titanium (Ti) and zinc (Zn) have been reported to enhance the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys [,] by promoting the formation of intermetallic phases that act as corrosion barriers [,]. In combination with Zn, Ti can form stable intermetallic compounds, such as Ti2Zn and TiZn16, which provide a shielding effect and limit the progression of corrosion fronts [,]. In contrast, micro-galvanic effects between intermetallics and the Mg matrix, arising from electrochemical potential differences, can accelerate localized corrosion [,]. For example, Ti rich intermetallics may act as cathodic sites, enhancing the localized anodic dissolution of Mg [,]. This makes the spatial distribution, morphology, and size of these phases critical for determining corrosion performance []. Consequently, Mg-Ti-Zn alloys are promising for applications requiring both biocompatibility and corrosion resistance, especially in medical devices, where controlled degradation minimizes toxic byproduct formation [,]. The MgTiZn (TZ) and Mg4TiZn (4TZ) alloys developed in this study demonstrated a rare combination of high hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance, which are often mutually exclusive in Mg-based systems. As illustrated in the schematic cross-sections (Figure 9), the TZ alloy exhibited a microstructure containing abundant intermetallic phases (Ti2Zn and Mg21Zn25) within a Ti- and Zn-enriched matrix (confirmed by the STEM analysis) and fine oxide particles (TiOx and MgO). In contrast, 4TZ presented a more homogeneous Mg-rich matrix containing solid solution domains composed of Mg, Ti, and Zn, and larger Ti rich regions. The presence of Ti and Zn in the matrix, along with uniformly distributed fine intermetallics, promoted the formation of a protective surface film (observed via XPS), leading to passivation and high corrosion resistance. Although micropores were observed in both alloys (Figure 1), which are typically expected to increase corrosion susceptibility, the corrosion current densities of the alloys remained low, suggesting that the protective effect of passivating surface films and refined microstructures outweighed the detrimental influence of porosity. cited_evidence.text: Our results indicated that kinetics of phase transformation plays a crucial role in phase selection of the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA. The phases can be controlled using kinetic ways according to the CCT curve. It seems that the sluggish diffusion in HEAs did not affect the kinetic behavior in this alloy system especially in the intermediate temperature. In fact, kinetic effect not only works for the special CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA but affects the phase selection of all HEAs. Li et al. reported that BCC phase can be obtained by supercooling method in the well-known FCC single phase CoCrFeNi HEA and the mechanical properties of the HEA was enhanced by three times. The rapid solidification behavior of CoCrCuNiFex HEA was also studied and useful nano-phases were found in the matrix, which would unquestionably strengthen the HEA dramatically. Ravi et al. reported that synthesis route can have a significant influence on the process of phase-choice and -evolution in different HEAs and this is actually a result of kinetic effect.
